case_info.scenario: A 61-year-old man presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, and persistent globus sensation. He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, cough, or hemoptysis. He had a history of coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, peripheral vascular disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and ulcerative colitis. He reported no immunosuppressive therapy. He quit smoking 8 months prior after a 35–pack-year history and consumed alcohol infrequently. He denied recent travel, exposure to tuberculosis, or prior radiation to the head and neck. On physical examination, there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes or oropharyngeal abnormalities. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a fibrinous, ulcerative lesion on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis with surrounding edema and preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility. Given concern for cancer, the patient underwent direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Examination under anesthesia confirmed irregular mucosa with fibrinous exudate localized to the epiglottis. Histopathology results revealed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Figure, A). Grocott methenamine silver stain highlighted narrow-based budding yeast (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Acutely inflamed, denuded laryngeal squamous mucosa with submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation (original magnification ×100). B, Biopsy demonstrating oval yeast forms consistent withHistoplasma capsulatum(arrowheads) measuring 2 to 4 μm in diameter with narrow-based budding (original magnification ×400).
case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

next reply.

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.

  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.

       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. 1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"

       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.
